pitch_detail.notes: A flake that faces left, climbed up to 5.10a, starts the route in the zigzag weaknesses left of the main roof on the Rabbits Coat wall.
Short face climbing, graded between 5.10b and 5.10c.
Called The Pillar; climbs at 5.9.
Called Groo-V; a groove at 5.8.
A big left-facing corner, dirty and with no protection, graded 5.10d to 5.11a. The hardest pitch of the route.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches from the one-line grade summary; no lengths, bolts or anchors given so none written, and notes are short for that reason.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin on the lower scoop at a small horizontal fault, marked by a single bolt, working up through a bushy corner containing a dead tree that leans. Climb the slab to the rocky headwall, trend right past a bolt to the big slanting terrace, and belay at the headwall station.
Move left and around to a long left-facing corner. Near the top, transfer up and right onto a broader face past a few bolts and top out on the ledge.
Begin out to the right on the face and climb bolts to a steep featured wall with twin cracks. The 40 m can be done as two 20 m pitches or as one linked lead.

review.changed: Wrote 3 entries: P1, P2 and P3-4 as one linked lead, since the text gives a single 40 m length and grade for them; stored count is 4. P1 has no grade or length in the text.

pitch_detail.anchor: station at base of dark streak
pitch_detail.notes: The start is on the second horizontal fault, a broad sandy ledge across the lower wall, with a single bolt in a small corner under the dark streak. Climb the face left of the streak with three bolts and some gear, then continue easily to the station at the foot of the streak on the main wall. Traversing 20 m right from the start of Tiramisu to a one-bolt station skips this pitch.
Steep going on big holds, cracks and a little slab for 35 m.
Up steeply again through a fist and hand crack, over overlapping rib features, then trending left to the top anchor. The length is quoted as both 25 m and 30 m.

review.changed: Wrote all 3 pitches. P3 length omitted since the text gives two values.

pitch_detail.notes: Same start as Creme Caramel: the end of the sandy vegetated ledge, with one bolt marking the beginning. Right-facing corners lead through an overlap, then veer right up steep blocks and cracks to a large ledge.
Undercling out left past a bolt, then arc up toward an obvious white scar with another bolt, and continue to the bolted station.
Climb steeply out right past a bolt, and keep going on similar ground above with good holds, bolts and whatever gear you can find.

Begin at a short left-facing corner just right of some steep roofs. Climb to a short roof, pull it, and continue up a lovely corner with laybacks, jams and jugs to a good belay ledge below a steep corner system. Reached after about 60 m of low-fifth scrambling above the tree bands; orange tat hangs from a tree at the ledge.
A thin corner system rises directly above the belay to a small roof. Two pitons protect the crack. Belay on a good ledge with a small tree.
Climb another short corner system right on the ridge, then scramble short, exposed steps for as long as rope drag allows.
Go over a small step, with the huge upper headwall looming ahead, and downclimb the far side to the good ledge below the hero pitch. The easier alternative approach joins here.

The hero pitch is an obvious crack up the ridge's left side whose width runs from fingers through hands and fists into offwidth. It takes gear to #4, and an old hex and an old piton are visible. Belay at the top of the crack.
Choose your own line up the ridge by the easiest path, over short steps mostly on the right, until you reach the base of the final headwall.
Quartzite on the left side of the headwall gives superb climbing.

review.changed: Wrote 7 entries for the stored 8 pitches: P6 and P7 are described as one 80 m stretch and written as '6-7'. Two further 5.9/5.10 pitches on the direct approach below the ledge are mentioned but not described, so not written.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.10 agrees with the hardest pitch. Stored length is null.

pitch_detail.notes: Start at the base of the big 'V' and take its left fork through excellent hand jams, pulling a small roof and continuing to a belay on a ramp.

A small finger-crack dihedral sits above the belay; climb about 15 m, then step left into an easier crack slanting up and left, using bushes to finish at a belay ledge. Two similar dihedrals start the pitch; use the left one, since the right does not reach the slanting crack.
Ramble up and right over unobvious ground, crossing a couple of pedestals into broken, lightly vegetated cracks.
Go up and right to a narrow, lush belay ledge.
A sustained lieback and stemming pitch in a thin corner.
Few details are recorded for this pitch beyond its grade, so expect to find the line yourself.
Easy blocky ground leads to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 7 entries; P7-8 are given a single grade and description so written as one. P6 has a grade but no description (the source itself has question marks).
review.other_findings: Stored 5.10c and 8 pitches agree. The ~20 m rappel on the descent is not a station list, so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Undercling the ramp slanting up to the right, round a couple of corners to a bush, then up to a flat belay ledge.

A huge pitch with dynamic, exciting moves. A broken corner on the right leads onto a thin face, where you slab out left to a jug and reach a foot across to the slab ramp. Stemming on thin opposing edges takes you past a welded nut halfway, then a short move left through overlaps; gear is thin but dependable. Finish by crossing hard right over horns to a hanging belay. The belay block is loose, so go higher into the corner to place better gear.
A pumpy layback up the 5.11b corner, straightforward moves, with lichen to contend with.

A large pocket split by a #2 crack lies right of the belay. Pull the bulge and head into less obvious terrain, with finger cracks and thin edges bearing up and slightly left, to a semi-hanging belay after roughly 35 m.
A somewhat loose crack of varying width goes up a short corner and then the face. The start is cruxy, then it eases to a belay in broken, jagged ground.
Move left to a short, comparatively easy finger crack, then break out onto easy terrain. Linking it with P7 is worthwhile.
Easy 5.6 ground; climb as far as you can, belay, then scramble to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote all 7 pitches. Grades are the first-ascent grades quoted in the source. P4's 35 m is stated as approximate.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.11b and 7 pitches agree. Descent is a ~20 m rappel plus scrambling, no station list.

pitch_detail.notes: Start at the ledge's right end on a wide crack. Hold right at first, then shift left around a small roof sitting in a wide chimney. Where it eases, drift right to a large blocky ledge system and set the belay at its right-hand end.

Descend a step and move right into the gash, then climb about 15 m. The gash's right wall gives powerful moves on an undercling crack with juggy sidepulls; easier cracks then lead to a comfortable ledge that holds a pair of fixed nuts.
A slot, then moderate cracks, lead to a slung pillar where the wall gets steeper. This pitch is often wet.
Known as the Youth Team Eliminator. Flared cracks and small roofs make for a struggle with multiple cruxes, ending at a large ledge under a right-facing corner that has two bolts.
A fine corner to stem, ending at a small stance with a bolt and a fixed pin. Sustained.
The corner steepens and passes a chimney, ending at a stance with two bolts.

Nicknamed the Murder of the Impussible. Go 20 m up the corner, step right, and climb a big flake for 5 m to its top. Then traverse right on very thin holds past two bolts to a crack, where a hanging belay is bolted.
A seam goes straight up past a bolt and two pins. Get over the roof on its right side and reach a stance on a small flake that is loose.
Hollow, steep flakes and cracks lead to a belay below a giant corner facing right.
Climb flared cracks to the top of the corner and belay at a semi-hanging stance.
Wander left and up over easier ground by whichever line is simplest, reaching a big flat ledge.
Starting at the ledge's right side, take a chimney, then lower-angle cracks that bear up and slightly left.
A short, enjoyable scramble on featured rock leads to the Minaret's summit.

review.changed: Wrote all 13 pitches to the Minaret summit. The seven further 5.9 pitches on the East Ridge of South Howser Tower (p14-20) are not described one by one, so not written.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.12c, but the two hardest pitches are stated as 5.12+ (the source mentions a first 5.12c pitch without placing it). Stored 13 pitches and length 594 m vs about 570 m of stated pitch lengths. Descent is by the standard South Howser Tower rappels, not listed.

pitch_detail.notes: The route starts at the top of the loose gully (keep right to avoid loose blocks). Ascend the obvious cracks and steps in the centre of the buttress, trending left to a belay at a tree snag.
Go straight up, left of the obvious white rock, staying right of a steep broken right-facing feature and exiting at an overlap to the face above. Belay on a terrace.
Climb the face's left side where gear is available, step right and girth-hitch the horizontal flake nicknamed the Cadbury flake, then continue up to a belay terrace.
A good corner system facing left accepts solid cams; layback and jam up it, leaving by easier ground to the next belay terrace.

Move up easy fifth class right of the buttress centre toward fine views of the Rampart arete. Then climb ledges up and left of the arete to the foot of a vertical crack. It runs out onto a blank face, where a delicate face move reaches the next terrace.
Broken ground and easy fifth class with the odd 5.7 move. Scramble a short way over loose ground to the toe of the next face, using the plumbline under a high rock outcrop as a belay reference.
Climb the left side of the face for gear, step back onto the face below the outcrop, and pass it on the right to reach the summit, a few metres from the high-point cairn.

review.changed: Wrote all 7 pitches. Belays are on terraces; no fixed anchors. Descent is a long walk-off along ridges, not rappels.

pitch_detail.notes: Scramble blocky terrain; most climbers will be happy soloing it.
More blocky ground, slightly more sustained than the first.
The real climbing starts here, with a choice of many cracks splitting the slab.
Further splitters up the slab, every crack eventually opening to chimney width beneath the large horizontal break that slices across the ridge. Sling the slab's corner on the right to make the belay.
Pull onto a lichen-covered slab with thin gear, then traverse left and down below a small tower on the ridge, setting up under the final crack.
The slanting inset crack is awkward at first, then the final hand crack lets you stem off the right wall if needed. Easily the best pitch.

review.changed: Wrote all 6 pitches. Descent is a scramble down the SW slopes.

pitch_detail.notes: Enter the gully directly when the snow cone is tall enough, or use a shallow corner trending right. Steep moves lead to a wide ledge.
Scramble right across wide ledges to the foot of a short, steep wall.
Climb the wall and several short steps.
The gully narrows here and the route climbs its back wall on excellent rock, taking a series of short steps.
Climb direct up an excellent face to a belay ledge.
A water-polished corner, or cracks to its left, lead to an alcove.
Stem out of the alcove and climb a corner, then go direct.
The couloir pinches into a chimney above the belay. Leave it by going left up a steep wall, reaching a gully with some loose stone.
Go straight up the gully to a steep step and some exciting moves up a corner slab.
More slab, then blocky ground to the crest of the upper west ridge. A scramble along the upper ridge reaches the summit.

review.changed: Wrote all 10 pitches; grades only where stated; no lengths, bolts or anchors given. The descent follows the regular route down the south face.

pitch_detail.notes: At the bottom of the buttress, scramble an obvious ramp leaning left and set up a belay (4th class), then continue straight up on a long pitch of low fifth class.
Easy ground leads to the buttress crest's left side, then up a prominent left-facing corner, easy to spot from the bivy, to a large ledge.

Continue up the corner system, starting on a face crack about a metre left of the corner crack. Follow it until you can traverse right across the corner crack and out of the system, then climb straight up until drag gets annoying. The traverse is about 5.7 PG for the follower.

One long pitch ends the roped climbing on the lower buttress. Afterward scramble up to the smooth ledge system under the large rectangular snowfield's lower-right corner, then traverse left beneath the snowfield to its lower-left corner (3rd/4th class). Several meltwater streams cross these ledges all day.

Pick a line onto the big ledge or ramp system above; starting further left gives more gear. Follow the easy ledges rightward, snowfield on your right, until they turn an outside corner, and belay there or continue about 7 m more if snow does not block it. The extra distance puts you under a big corner in the left wall, visible from the bivy site.

The big corner has little protection for a long way, so first traverse back left 7 m to the start of a right-trending crack or ramp with a tricky start. That leads to the corner. Climb five metres of it, past a piton, to a ledge system on the right, then continue right along easier ground and belay before the main giant face, level with an obvious horizontal crack crossing it.

Move a few metres left to the huge face's left edge, then cross right along the obvious horizontal break, clipping an awkwardly low bolt and then stepping down to an inverted pin. Holds are best above the crack. Belay at the first clear corner facing left.
Climb the corner, then take an easy ramp rising right for most of a rope length. Once the rock above the ramp turns smoother with fewer features, build your belay.
About 40 m above the belay are two wide, shallow roofs at the same height, roughly 10 m apart. Aim for the left one, meandering along weaknesses, and belay about 10 m short of it.

Long runouts; two extra bolts (one before and one after the existing one) would help. Go over the small roof on the left, where gear is good, and keep following the weakness as it drifts left. A couple of loose pins may be passed, then a stainless bolt roughly 30 m out; ignore the pins. Find the easiest line for about 15 m without gear to a horizontal crack across the face. Move right a little until it becomes a small ledge, and climb the easy cracks above to find gear for a belay.

Climb the easy crack system trending slightly left, with many options, to a big ledge system about 3 m deep under a huge roof. Move right along it to a belay or bivy bolt. Some long runouts on easy ground; the bivy ledge is mediocre but gets brief morning sun.

Traverse up and right beneath a right-facing roof or corner toward the upper-right end of the giant roof system. Step right onto the well-featured face and continue up and a little left to a good belay ledge with gear. There may be no good protected belay for the next easy 20-30 m.

Climb easily up and left on featured rock to where the face steepens (about 30 m). Then climb the continuous, reasonably protected steeper face to the next change to even steeper rock. You can belay there, but it is better to traverse left about 5 m to a more comfortable stance with plenty of gear. Protection is not obvious before that traverse.

Continue the leftward traverse past an obvious fresh white scar, then pull 3-4 committing moves up and left and belay inside a large corner facing right. Staying horizontal to the corner skips those moves, then climb a few metres to the belay. The corner can be wet in any summer month.

About 10 easy metres up the corner is a big roof. At its base, hand-traverse left under it for 2 m (good gear) to another large right-facing corner and belay for better communication and less drag. A harder leftward traverse higher in the corner has been done but is wetter.
The corner system above is steep and exposed with good holds and reasonable gear. Belay after roughly 30 m, or link into the next pitch.

Several options in the corner all lead to a distinctive belay spot. The rock above looks worse and harder, but a shallow roof on the left wall can be traversed; where its left end meets a wide face crack, the crack narrows to hand size above, out of sight from the belay. An easier variant wanders left into a different corner and returns to merge with this pitch.

Undercling the shallow roof leftward for 2-3 m to the crack system in the left wall. Where the traverse arrives, it becomes a corner hiding a hand crack. Follow that and a sharp arete upward along weaknesses, eventually curving right onto the huge summit slab.
Many friction, crack and ramp options exist on this big clean face. Start with 30 m up the left corner of the face, with abundant protection.
Continue up the corner a short way, then branch out onto the face. Plenty of options, with large ledge systems crisscrossing the face.
A large, easy ramp angling right takes you to the slab's right edge, a scenic spot with an excellent bivy site.

review.changed: Wrote the 21 pitches the text describes one by one; the stored count is 23 and no description exists for pitches 22-23. Pitch 16-17 alternative folded into notes. Descent (hidden rappel station on the east edge of the summit, then the east ridge) is not a station list, so no rappel table.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.10- R matches the hardest stated grade 5.10a roughly. The route is described as 23 pitches on a 60 m rope; only 21 are given. Only 3 bolts in total on the route.

pitch_detail.notes: A gear lead and an easy start to the day. The belay is in the rock scoop between the two ponds. Angle up and left to a right-facing finger crack with good gear on its underside, though it is fragile where it thins at the top. Use long runners on this full 60 m pitch. Go straight up toward the darker stone for the belay; one more piece is optional at the ledge before the first station.
Pad up the slab toward a large horn high and left. One bolt and an old piton lie midway. Look for the station on your right in small dishes as you near the feature.
Protect the move around the horn, then go straight up toward flowery cracks with good gear. Clip one bolt before stepping up and left to the next level. Drop nothing in the cracks.
A gear lead straight up small breaks, with good protection above. Watch for the station in a brown horizontal seam once the pitch flattens.
Go up toward a bolt near the darker band at 30 m, then drift slightly left. Pad toward the large ledge and continue up and left to the station by the right-facing crack.
Keep left of the larger roofs on the right. You can either step up over the overlap, or work left and then back right around the corner.
Step right just above the bulge at the station, place something in the left-facing corner and go straight up easy ground.
Scramble up and right over broken rock, drop a piece in on the right, then find an easy way over to the anchors. The leftward traverse to the anchors is often wet, so pick your line with care.

Aim straight at the UFO. One piece goes in on the right at the first bulge, then climb up its middle. Protect the committing steps in the exact centre that put you on top, then pad directly to the station.
Follow lighter-colored rock up and left toward the high bulge.
Aim for breaks in the rock above, clipping a bolt at the first bulge. Protect the featured but polished section, then go back left to find the station.

Go directly over the block's centre; the move is enjoyable and protects well. Work up the cracks right of the bushes and finish in a small dish. The rock right of this bulge is rotten, so the centre is the best way.

Climb straight to a bolt just above a small black bulge, then a second bolt, and plan your move right into the dirty trough. Messy seams above offer a couple of good placements through the worst of it into the junipers. Trend right at the trough's top, slinging stumps as needed. The station is straight above the trough, reached by crossing a ledge from right to left.

Adventure climbing. Left of the station, go straight up two veins to a juniper island, staying left of it to reach the whale's back. Sling a tree or two if needed and go left up the whale's back for an easier approach to the small ledge above; gear is optional halfway up on the right. On the ledge, clip the first bolt, trend right to the second, then right toward the opening in the greenery. A chained station sits above a small trough in white rock. If you are not going to the summit, this is where you rappel from.

There is no station on this pitch. Sling as many trees as you like, bear right from the station on rock, then go directly up into the open meadow. From there it is about 200 m of sustained 4th/5th class over tree ledges, moss grooves and dirty cracks to the summit; going on commits you to walking off.

review.changed: Wrote 15 entries: all 14 stored pitches plus the optional 55 m meadow pitch. The chained-station rappel with two 60 m ropes is stated generally, with no station list, so no rappel table.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.8- and 14 pitches; the hardest stated grade is 5.8+ (P13), and the text describes an extra pitch 15 to the meadow.

pitch_detail.notes: Locate the large right-facing dihedral at the buttress's left side and thread through one of the smaller corners to a shallow diagonal ledge under the dihedral's arete.
Get onto the arete and follow it up to the very large sandy ledge.

Think about moving the belay to the foot of the smaller arete at the sandy ledge's outer end, on the left of the whole buttress's main arete. Steep cracks in good granite lead up it to a little niche of very rotten rock; squeeze in and set a belay on the better rock at the back.

Step left out of the niche back onto bombproof granite. One 5.10 move, or a French-free pull, takes you left of the small arete into two cracks. Above that, excellent rock follows as the cracks merge and then split again, a second crack appearing on the right in a shallow corner over a small bulge, which holds the grade down. As the two cracks diverge, step right onto ledgier ground, scramble the chossy stretch, and pick a belay.

Continue through the loose zone, then up steeper, burly hand cracks that split blocks between ledges, ending on a flat ledge beneath an airy arete to the left. You could link this with the next pitch.

Step left into the notch separating the belay from the arete's airy edge. A technical crack on the left edge of the arete's face leads to a bombay chimney, beneath which you step right. Place a cam and wiggle up the chimney into easier terrain, then scramble to the ridge top. After that, 3rd-4th class scrambling returns to the talus.

review.changed: Wrote 6 pitches; the text describes six while the stored count is 5.
review.other_findings: Stored count 5, text gives 6 pitches. P4 has a single 5.10 move (or French-free) in a pitch graded 5.9, above the stored route grade of 5.9.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin a few feet left of the clear right-facing corner and climb several small steps. The rock is solid but coated in lichen and a thin flaking layer. Belay at the big pine under a V-shaped roof.

Traverse slightly right and layback the flake under the roof, cross the roof at its middle and use the small finger crack on the right (the flakes on the left look unreliable). Top out on a short, lichen-coated, crumbly slab and belay on the big ledge under the tower.

Shift a few feet right and head directly to a left-facing corner coated in lichen, right of a yellow roof and just under a big pine. This crux gives the route its name: a brief crack sequence in the lichenous corner, with crumbly rock that makes footwork difficult. Protection is easy and secure until the exit, which calls for chicken-winging, mantling or riding the final bulge. Belay at the pine.
Take the corner that starts at the pine and goes up and right to the ridge top. Belay on top.

review.changed: Wrote all 4 pitches; lengths converted from feet.

pitch_detail.notes: Great chimney and layback climbing. With a 60 m rope you must belay at the big pine, which is full of ants. In the shade in the morning.
Scramble to where the wall steepens and an old piton shows. Belaying here avoids rope drag, although P2 and P3 can be linked into a 75 m pitch that proves awkward.
Take the short wall to the right and continue right over slabs to the crooked piton. Pass it and go up to two small pines. Sunny in late morning.
Easy slabs steepen, and cracks take you to the tree at the left foot of the final headwall.

The crux. Take the overhanging wide crack roughly 20 ft right of the large right-facing offwidth corner on the headwall's left end. It begins overhanging and dirty, with slippery lichen and thin crumbling rock, yet is easy to protect with big cams (#1-4), and footholds are nearly useless. When it widens beyond even a #6, make desperate moves right to a flake that takes a #0.5 and #0.3. Keep traversing right and climb a flared, shallow corner that accepts only tiny 000 and 00 cams in two shallow holes about 15 ft apart. Set a belay as soon as good cracks appear, watching rope drag on the low traverse. Sunny.
Go up and left over easy slabs to the foot of a corner whose crack is harder than it looked from below. Get through it and finish up the right-facing corner to the top.

review.changed: Wrote all 6 pitches; lengths converted from feet. The walk-off is the Devil's Slide trail to Humber Park, about 1.5 hours.

pitch_detail.notes: Orange, featured rock with puzzling moves above gear that is sometimes poor. Make a belay by lassoing a horn, saving a hand-size piece for it. A full 60 m pitch.
Go up and right from the belay, round the arete into a hand crack, and belay at the foot of a corner.
Go up the flaky corner to a stance on top of a pillar.
The leaning splitter finger crack leads to the east ridge; belay when you can. It could be combined with P3.
A fun ridge climb to the summit, over 60 m, where simul-climbing may be sensible.

review.changed: Wrote all 5 pitches. P5 length (60+ m) omitted as open-ended.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin in a flaky corner system and get past a little roof to a belay ledge equipped with bolts.
Climb the major corner system, sometimes branching onto grooved cracks on either side.

Climb the corner to a pedestal, then layback the left-hand crack. Move over to the right wall below the roof features, then up and across beneath the second tier of roofs to the bolted belay. A follower stayed in the left vertical cracks and avoided the roofs altogether, for sustained layback power at around 5.11.

Angle up and left from the anchor on flakes and pull into a layback with a thin crack in the back. Lay back flared cracks to good stances on the left. Pull over a bulge through more flared hand cracks, mantle, then trend up and right to a good sandy belay with bolts.
Stem up the corner crack to the top out. The walk-off goes left down a nice sandy slope.

review.changed: Wrote all 5 pitches; lengths converted from feet. P3 and P4 share the top grade so no crux flagged.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb blocks into a corner facing right, then follow hand cracks up the face to a short, easy chimney ramp, passing a ledge on the left wall. Keep going up the chimney until you can link hand cracks and generous footholds over the face to an exposed stance at the arete's outer edge on the right, where you belay.
Hand cracks lead to a sloping ledge you can see from the ground, which offers another exposed stance on the arete's outer edge.

Hand cracks reach the top of the orange face, then the top of the tower. Sling a well-placed horn above it, then downclimb or traverse out right on a foot ledge into a hand crack in a corner facing left. That corner makes up the left side of a pillar like a candlestick. Follow it to a higher ledge and belay; running the rope from the tower straight to that ledge prevents drag.

Keep going up the pillar, then bear right through cracks and flakes, skipping the face above the pillar with its wedged blocks, and bear left to a belay inside a corner facing right, just under the blocky west arete.
Follow the corner on cracks and jugs, going straight through the summit blocks above that are split apart. Descend gentle slopes along the west ridge.

review.changed: Wrote all 5 pitches; no grades, lengths or bolts stated per pitch, so none written.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.9, 5 pitches; no per-pitch grade in the source.

skip_reasons.bc_west_ear_helix: Text gives only one-line grades per pitch (P1 5.8, P2 5.6, P3 5.7, P4 5.8, P5 5.3, P6 5.6, all under 50 m), no per-pitch description.
